Polynomial

 Home Mathematics Area of mathematics Algebra
OurBigBook.com Words: 5k Articles: 94
A polynomial is a finite sum of monomials with coefficients in a ring. In one variable X over a commutative ring R, write
p(X)=a0​+a1​X+⋯+an​Xn,aj​∈R.
(1)
The symbol X is an indeterminate: it records powers formally before we choose an input value. Finite expressions are easy to add, multiply, evaluate, and differentiate, making polynomials a common language for exact algebra and approximate numerical analysis.
Consider the real polynomial
p(X)=X3−3X2+4=(X+1)(X−2)2.
(2)
The expanded form displays the coefficients and the degree of a polynomial; the factored form displays its roots of a polynomial. At X=3, either description gives p(3)=4. At X=−1 and X=2, the factored form makes the zero values immediate. Keeping several descriptions of one object is useful because each makes a different question easy.
The graph shows another connection. The factor X+1 changes sign across −1, while (X−2)2 stays nonnegative across 2. Thus the graph crosses the axis at the simple root of a polynomial and touches it at the double root. Multiplicity of a root turns an algebraic repetition into visible local behavior.
For calculations, Horner's method evaluates a polynomial through nested multiplication. For modeling, a Taylor polynomial describes local behavior near a point, while polynomial interpolation constructs a polynomial matching prescribed data. Their usefulness comes with assumptions: a local approximation and an exact identity are different claims, and changing the coefficient ring can change which polynomial roots exist.

Factorization of polynomials

Words: 32
Polynomial OurBigBook.com
A polynomial factorization expresses a polynomial as a product of other polynomials. The allowed coefficients matter: X2−2 has no nonconstant factorization over the rational numbers, but factors as (X−2​)(X+2​) over the real numbers. Difference of squares gives X2−Y2=(X−Y)(X+Y) over any commutative ring.

Polynomial evaluation (Ea​(p)=p(a))

Words: 56
Polynomial OurBigBook.com
Polynomial evaluation replaces the indeterminate of a polynomial by an input value. For a fixed scalar a, the rule Ea​:p↦p(a) is a linear functional on a vector space of polynomials, because evaluating a linear combination gives the same linear combination of the values. For p(t)=1+2t+3t2, evaluation at zero gives one and evaluation at two gives seventeen. Polynomial interpolation uses these measurements to reconstruct a polynomial subject to a polynomial degree bound.

Indeterminate (X)

Words: 30
Polynomial OurBigBook.com
An indeterminate is a formal symbol used to construct a polynomial. Choosing an input later defines a polynomial function; the symbol itself is not a fixed member of the coefficient ring.

Additive polynomial (L(X+Y)=L(X)+L(Y))

Words: 253 Articles: 3
Polynomial OurBigBook.com
Over a field of characteristic p, additive polynomials are sums of p-power monomials, L(X)=∑i​ai​Xpi. They act linearly over the prime field. The identity follows from the Frobenius endomorphism; the converse follows by comparing mixed binomial coefficients. Their zero sets are additive groups, and a nonzero linear coefficient makes all roots simple.

Linearized polynomial over a finite field (L(X)=∑i=0d​ai​Xqi)

Words: 201 Articles: 2
Additive polynomial OurBigBook.com
Over a field containing Fq​, a sum of q-power monomials is Fq​-linear. If its leading coefficient and linear coefficient are nonzero, its root space has exactly qd elements and dimension d over Fq​. Automorphisms of its splitting field act faithfully and linearly on that root space, embedding the Galois group in GL(d,q).

Quadratic constant extension of a q-squared linearized splitting field (Gal(E/Fq2​(T))◃Gal(E/Fq​(T)))

Words: 70
Linearized polynomial over a finite field OurBigBook.com
For even d=2n, the roots of Xqd+Xq2+TX form an n-dimensional vector space over Fq2​. Ratios (cα)/α for a nonzero root α show that the splitting field contains every c∈Fq2​. The subgroup fixing that quadratic constant extension is normal of index two and lies in GL(n,q2); applying projective transitivity over Fq2​(T) makes it contain SL(n,q2). It therefore normalizes that special linear group, while the full group acts semilinearly.

Projective transitivity of a trinomial linearized polynomial (L(X)=Xqd+Xq+TX)

Words: 76
Linearized polynomial over a finite field OurBigBook.com
For d≥2, nonzero roots define projective-point coordinates s=Xq−1, satisfying sN+s+T=0, where N=(qd−1)/(q−1). This polynomial is irreducible over Fq​(T). After fixing one root s, the remaining coordinates satisfy R(Y,s)=(YN−sN)/(Y−s)+1. Substitute z=Y/s and h=1/s: the equation becomes hN−1+(zN−1)/(z−1)=0. At a nontrivial Nth root of unity the second term has a simple zero, so the polynomial is Eisenstein over the algebraic closure's rational function field. This proves irreducibility of R and hence two-transitivity on projective points.

Hasse derivative (f[ℓ](x)=∑j≥ℓ​(ℓj​)fj​xj−ℓ)

Words: 56
Polynomial OurBigBook.com
The Hasse derivatives of a polynomial are the coefficients in f(x+t)=∑ℓ≥0​f[ℓ](x)tℓ. A point a has multiplicity at least m exactly when f[ℓ](a)=0 for 0≤ℓ<m. Unlike iterated formal derivatives divided by factorials, this definition works in positive characteristic, where factorials can vanish. For example, in characteristic two (x+1)2 has zero first formal derivative but nonzero second Hasse derivative.

Horner's method

Words: 227
Polynomial OurBigBook.com
Horner's method evaluates a polynomial by nested multiplication, requiring one multiplication and one addition per degree after initialization.
For p(X)=an​Xn+⋯+a0​, start with bn​=an​ and compute bj​=xbj+1​+aj​ for j=n−1,…,0. The final value is b0​=p(x). Equivalently,
p(x)=a0​+x(a1​+x(a2​+⋯+xan​)).
(3)
This reorganization reuses intermediate results, avoiding separate computation of every power. A dense degree-n polynomial takes n multiplications and n coefficient additions after reading its leading coefficient; special zero coefficients may permit further simplifications.
For our cubic, the coefficient list in descending order is 1,−3,0,4. The zero is important: it occupies the missing X term's position. At x=2, the accumulated values are
1 ⟶ 2⋅1−3=−1 ⟶ 2(−1)+0=−2 ⟶ 2(−2)+4=0.
(4)
At x=3, the same operations give 1,0,0,4, confirming p(3)=4.
The intermediate values do more than evaluate. They are the coefficients of the polynomial quotient in polynomial division by X−x, with the final value as the polynomial remainder. At x=2, the first three values give X2−X−2, so
p(X)=(X−2)(X2−X−2)+0.
(5)
At x=3, they give X2, so p(X)=(X−3)X2+4. This links an efficient numerical calculation with the exact factor theorem.
William George Horner's 1819 paper concerns solving numerical equations by successive approximation. The Royal Society archive records the manuscript and its reading on 1 July 1819; it provides a historical reference for the method's name. [ref]

Fixed-degree polynomial limit

Words: 72
Polynomial OurBigBook.com
If polynomials of degree at most d converge at d+1 distinct points, their coefficients converge, by invertibility of the Vandermonde matrix. Their limit is a polynomial of degree at most d, and convergence is uniform on every compact subset of C. Under convergence on compact sets, Rouché's theorem further locates a unique nearby zero for each simple root of the limit, for all sufficiently large indices. Finite initial polynomials need not have any root.

Quadratic polynomial (ax2+bx+c,a=0)

Words: 34
Polynomial OurBigBook.com
A quadratic polynomial in one variable over a field has polynomial degree two and the displayed form. Its roots of a polynomial satisfy a quadratic equation. The polynomial and its associated polynomial function are distinct objects: over a finite field, different polynomials can define the same function.

Polynomial identity (P(x)=Q(x))

Words: 64
Polynomial OurBigBook.com
A polynomial identity is equality of two polynomials for every value of the variables, rather than an equation imposed only at selected roots. Over the real or complex numbers, this is equivalent to equality of corresponding coefficients: their difference, if nonzero, has only finitely many roots in one variable. The binomial theorem is an example. Coefficient comparison transfers a polynomial product identity into finite sums of binomial coefficients.

Coprime polynomials (gcd(f,g)=1)

Words: 126 Articles: 1
Polynomial OurBigBook.com
Two polynomials over a field are coprime if their only common factors are nonzero constants. Equivalently, their greatest common divisor is a unit in the polynomial ring. In one variable this is equivalent to a Bezout identity Af+Bg=1 with polynomial coefficients. Independent members of a pencil spanned by coprime polynomials are themselves coprime.

Polynomial pencil with four square members

Words: 84
Coprime polynomials OurBigBook.com
Let u,v∈C[t] be coprime polynomials. If αu+βv is a square for four distinct (α:β), then u,v are constant. For independent u,v, the four square members Lj​=sj2​ are pairwise coprime polynomials. Let d and e be their maximal and minimal degrees; at least three have degree d. For independent members of degrees e,d, the nonzero polynomial W=Lk′​Ll​−Lk​Ll′​ has degree at most d+e−1. Each sj​ divides W, giving degW≥(3d+e)/2>d+e−1, a contradiction. The dependent case follows directly from coprimality of polynomials.

Symmetric polynomial

Words: 27
Polynomial OurBigBook.com
A symmetric polynomial is unchanged by permutations of its variables. The Fundamental theorem of symmetric polynomials expresses it as a polynomial in the elementary symmetric polynomials. The square of the Vandermonde determinant is an important example.

Descartes' rule of signs (N+​(p)≤V(p))

Words: 139
Polynomial OurBigBook.com
Let V(p) be the number of sign changes in the list of nonzero coefficients of a real polynomial, arranged by increasing or decreasing degree. The positive roots of a polynomial, counted with multiplicity of a root, satisfy
N+​(p)≤V(p),V(p)−N+​(p) is even.
(6)
The bound follows by induction on the nonzero terms after removing the lowest power of x. Differentiation removes the constant coefficient. If it and the next coefficient have opposite signs, the Rolle root count with multiplicities loses at most one root and the sign-change count loses one. If their signs agree, the derivative must have an extra root before the first positive root, so neither count needs that extra allowance. The parity statement follows by comparing the signs near zero and at positive infinity: roots of odd multiplicity reverse the sign, and roots of even multiplicity preserve it. Apply the same rule to p(−x) to bound negative roots.

Even part of a polynomial ((P(z)+P(−z))/2)

Words: 28
Polynomial OurBigBook.com
The even part of a polynomial P is (P(z)+P(−z))/2. It retains exactly the terms whose exponents are even. Applied to the binomial theorem, it extracts sums of even-indexed binomial coefficients.

Leading coefficient of a polynomial (an​)

Words: 45
Polynomial OurBigBook.com
The leading coefficient of a nonzero polynomial an​xn+⋯+a0​, with an​=0, is an​; its degree of a polynomial is n. A monic polynomial has leading coefficient one. For polynomials over a field, a product has leading coefficient equal to the product of the two leading coefficients, which prevents cancellation of their highest-degree terms.

Polynomial factor (g∣f)

Words: 31
Polynomial OurBigBook.com
A polynomial factor g of a polynomial f satisfies f=gh for another polynomial h. Common polynomial factors are cancelled when expressing a rational function in reduced form; its degree of a rational map of the Riemann sphere is determined after this cancellation.

Coefficient extraction ([x1a1​​⋯xnan​​]P)

Words: 49
Polynomial OurBigBook.com
Coefficient extraction is the linear operation selecting the coefficient of a specified monomial from a polynomial or Laurent polynomial. Multiplying by the inverse of that monomial reduces the operation to taking a constant term. The coefficient form of the Combinatorial Nullstellensatz expresses certain coefficient extractions as weighted sums of evaluations on a finite product set.

Nonnegative polynomial

Words: 345 Articles: 4
Polynomial OurBigBook.com
A real polynomial is globally nonnegative if its value is nonnegative at every point of its real domain. A sum of squares polynomial is always nonnegative, but the Horn copositive matrix gives a nonnegative quartic polynomial that is not a sum of squares polynomial.

Polynomial SOS

Words: 313 Articles: 3
Nonnegative polynomial OurBigBook.com
A sum of squares polynomial is a real polynomial expressible as p=∑i​qi2​ for real polynomials qi​. In the homogeneous degree-2m case the summands may be taken homogeneous of degree m. Every such polynomial is nonnegative on real inputs; the converse fails for multivariate polynomials in general.
A real polynomial p is a sum of squares polynomial if p=∑ℓ​qℓ2​ for real polynomials qℓ​. Such a representation certifies global nonnegativity. If m(z) is the vector of relevant monomials, the identity p(z)=m(z)TGm(z) with a positive semidefinite matrix G encodes a sum of squares through a Gram matrix. Equating coefficients is linear in G, so finding a certificate is a semidefinite program.

Homogeneous sum of squares representation

Words: 53
Polynomial SOS OurBigBook.com
If a degree-2d homogeneous polynomial is a sum of squares polynomial, it has a representation as squares of degree-d homogeneous polynomials. In any sum of squares, the highest-degree terms cannot cancel, since their homogeneous part is itself a sum of squares. Likewise the lowest nonzero degree cannot cancel. Thus every nonzero summand has only degree d.

Sign averaging of a sum of squares

Words: 62
Polynomial SOS OurBigBook.com
A polynomial invariant under changing the sign of each coordinate can have its sum of squares representation averaged over independent Rademacher random variables εi​∈{−1,1}. Distinct parity patterns of monomials have zero cross terms because E[∏i​εiai​​] vanishes when some exponent is odd. For a quadratic homogeneous polynomial
q(z)=∑i​ai​zi2​+∑i<j​bij​zi​zj​,
(7)
this gives
E[q(ε1​z1​,…,εn​zn​)2]=(∑i​ai​zi2​)2+∑i<j​bij2​zi2​zj2​.
(8)
This identity separates the even monomials from each distinct two-coordinate parity pattern.

Sum of squares criterion for a biquadratic form

Words: 95
Polynomial SOS OurBigBook.com
For a real symmetric matrix A, set v(z)=(z12​,…,zn2​)T. Then
v(z)TAv(z) is a sum of squares⟺A=P+N,P⪰0,N=NT≥0 entrywise.
(9)
For sufficiency, factor P=BTB. Its contribution is a sum of squares of linear combinations of zi2​, while the contribution of N is ∑i​Nii​(zi2​)2+∑i<j​2Nij​(zi​zj​)2. For necessity, use a homogeneous sum of squares representation and sign averaging of a sum of squares. Writing each quadratic summand with coefficients aℓi​,bℓij​ gives P=∑ℓ​aℓ​aℓT​, Nii​=0 and Nij​=21​∑ℓ​bℓij2​ for i<j. Comparing coefficients gives A=P+N.
This is the basic semidefinite programming certificate of copositivity discussed in Parrilo's paper on matrix copositivity.

Polynomial function

Words: 192 Articles: 2
Polynomial OurBigBook.com
A polynomial function is the function obtained by evaluating a polynomial on a specified ring or field. Distinct polynomials can induce the same polynomial function over a finite field; for example, xp and x agree on Fp​.
Over F2​, the nonzero formal polynomial X2−X evaluates to zero at both possible inputs, zero and one. It therefore induces the same polynomial function as the zero polynomial, despite having different coefficients and polynomial degree. Over an infinite field, equality at every input forces equality of polynomials by the root bound for a polynomial. The distinction matters whenever a representation is supposed to identify the function uniquely.

Piecewise polynomial function

Words: 99 Articles: 1
Polynomial function OurBigBook.com
A piecewise polynomial function agrees with a polynomial on each member of a partition. Approximation claims usually require finitely many pieces with controlled interfaces. In one dimension, finitely many partition points and localized wavelets with more vanishing moments than the polynomial degree leave only a bounded number of nonzero coefficients per scale, yielding exponential squared best N-term approximation error.

Piecewise polynomial function OurBigBook.com
For integer r≥1, the truncated power is zero for x≤t and equals (x−t)r for x>t. It is globally Cr−1 and its rth derivative has a jump at t. Order zero is the step-function convention 1{x>t}​. Knot divided differences of these functions produce B-splines.

Laurent polynomial OurBigBook.com
For a nonzero Laurent polynomial, its breadth is the largest exponent with nonzero coefficient minus the smallest such exponent. Unlike its highest exponent, it is unchanged by multiplying by a Laurent monomial unit. The breadth of a nonzero constant is zero.

Laurent polynomial OurBigBook.com
A monomial allowing negative integer exponents in invertible variables. Finite sums of Laurent monomials form a Laurent polynomial ring. In a graded coordinate ring each has total degree ∑i​ai​.

Constant term (CT)

Words: 53
Laurent polynomial OurBigBook.com
The constant term of a Laurent polynomial is the coefficient of the monomial with exponent zero in every variable. Taking the constant term in just one variable leaves a Laurent polynomial in the other variables; successive extractions recover the full constant term. This operation is linear, but need not preserve products. The Dyson constant-term identity is a multivariate example of coefficient extraction.

A polynomial equation has the form p(x1​,…,xn​)=0 for a polynomial p. Its solutions are the points at which that polynomial vanishes.

Cubic equation

Polynomial equation OurBigBook.com
A cubic equation is a polynomial equation of degree of a polynomial three, ax3+bx2+cx+d=0, with a=0. Its three complex roots of a polynomial, counted with multiplicity of a root, need not all have physical significance in an application; a model often selects a branch by continuity from a known limit.

Monic polynomial

Words: 222 Articles: 3
Polynomial OurBigBook.com
A monic polynomial has leading coefficient one.

Monic polynomial division over a ring (g=qf+r,degr<degf)

Words: 215 Articles: 2
Monic polynomial OurBigBook.com
If f(T) is monic of degree k over a commutative ring, every polynomial has a unique expression g=qf+r with degr<k. Cancel the highest remaining term successively; the leading coefficient one needs no inversion. Uniqueness follows because multiplication by a monic polynomial raises the degree of every nonzero polynomial by k, even when the ring has zero divisors. The same argument applies to an even central variable and central coefficients in a graded commutative algebra.

Monic polynomial quotient is finite free (A[T]/(F)≅AdegF)

Words: 141 Articles: 1
Monic polynomial division over a ring OurBigBook.com
For any commutative ring A and a monic polynomial F of positive degree D, monic polynomial division over a ring gives unique representatives of degree less than D. Thus the classes of 1,T,…,TD−1 form a basis of a module over A. This is a finite free algebra, hence flat, and the map A→A[T]/(F) is injective. The monic hypothesis makes leading-degree arguments valid even when A has zero divisors.
Monic irreducible integer-polynomial quotient is a domain (Z[X]/(p))
Words: 82
Monic polynomial quotient is finite free OurBigBook.com
For monic p∈Z[X] irreducible in Q[X], monic division gives an injection Z[X]/(p)↪Q[X]/(p): an integer polynomial in the rational ideal has zero integer remainder. The target is a field, so the source is an integral domain. For positive degree d, unique remainders make the source a free abelian group on 1,X,…,Xd−1. The nonzero integer 2 is not a unit, since multiplying an integer remainder by two cannot give remainder one. Thus this integral domain is not a field.

Multivariate polynomial

Words: 339 Articles: 6
Polynomial OurBigBook.com
A multivariate polynomial is a finite linear combination of monomials in two or more variables.

Diagonal monomial action of a second-order Euler operator (x2∂x2​+y2∂y2​)

Words: 55
Multivariate polynomial OurBigBook.com
The monomial xiyj is an eigenvector of the differential linear operator x2∂x2​+y2∂y2​, with eigenvalue i(i−1)+j(j−1). Over the real or complex numbers this vanishes exactly for i,j∈{0,1}. On polynomials of bounded total degree, the kernel is therefore spanned by the permitted members of 1,x,y,xy, while the image of a linear map is spanned by all remaining monomials. The trace is the sum of those diagonal eigenvalues.

Alternating polynomial (P(xσ(1)​,…,xσ(m)​)=sgn(σ)P(x))

Words: 104 Articles: 1
Multivariate polynomial OurBigBook.com
Over a field of characteristic zero, an alternating polynomial changes sign when two variables are interchanged. It vanishes when two coordinates agree, so each factor xi​−xj​ divides it. These distinct linear factors are relatively prime in the polynomial ring, hence their product, the Vandermonde determinant, divides it. The quotient is a symmetric polynomial.

Monomial alternant (Aℓ​(x)=det(xiℓj​​))

Words: 56
Alternating polynomial OurBigBook.com
A monomial alternant is the determinant formed from powers with an integer exponent tuple ℓ. It is a polynomial when the exponents are nonnegative, and otherwise a Laurent polynomial. Equal exponents give equal columns and zero determinant; interchanging exponents changes its sign. Ordered strictly decreasing nonnegative exponents give a basis of alternating polynomials, by grouping monomials into permutation orbits.

Polynomial restriction to a line (Rℓ​f(t)=f(a+tv))

Words: 62
Multivariate polynomial OurBigBook.com
For a line ℓ={a+tv:t∈R} with v=0, restricting a degree-at-most-d multivariate polynomial gives a univariate polynomial in t of degree at most d. Its d+1 coefficients are linear functionals of the original coefficient vector. Vanishing on the whole line is therefore equivalent to at most d+1 homogeneous linear conditions. Alternatively, d+1 distinct roots force the restriction to be identically zero.

Dimension of a bounded-total-degree polynomial space (dimP≤d​(kn)=(nn+d​))

Words: 103 Articles: 1
Multivariate polynomial OurBigBook.com
The vector space of formal polynomials over a field k in n variables with total degree of a polynomial at most d has the monomial basis x1a1​​⋯xnan​​ for nonnegative exponents with ∑i​ai​≤d. Introducing a slack exponent and using stars and bars counts (nn+d​) basis elements. These are formal polynomials; over a finite field, distinct formal polynomials need not define distinct polynomial functions unless suitable degree restrictions hold.

Evaluation of bounded-degree multivariate polynomials on a finite set defines a linear map EP​:f↦(f(p))p∈P​. Its rank is at most ∣P∣ and its kernel is the space of polynomials vanishing on P. The rank-nullity theorem gives dimkerEP​≥(nd+n​)−∣P∣ for degree at most d in n variables. Dependent point constraints only enlarge the kernel.

Polynomial OurBigBook.com
A zero of a function f is an argument a for which f(a)=0.

Zero set (f−1({0}))

Words: 50
Zero of a function OurBigBook.com
The zero set of a function f is the preimage f−1({0}), consisting of all its zeros of a function. For a real- or complex-valued continuous function, it is a closed set, because the preimage of the closed singleton {0} under a continuous function is closed. A nonzero holomorphic function on a connected open set has isolated zeros by the identity theorem for holomorphic functions.

Root of a polynomial

Words: 595 Articles: 11
Zero of a function OurBigBook.com
A root of a polynomial f is a scalar a satisfying f(a)=0 in the chosen field or ring. For p(X)=(X+1)(X−2)2 over the real numbers, the distinct roots of a polynomial are −1 and 2. The second has multiplicity of a root two, so there are three roots when counted with multiplicity.
The domain matters. X2+1 has no real polynomial root, but has the two complex number roots i,−i. The fundamental theorem of algebra guarantees a polynomial root in the complex numbers for every nonconstant complex polynomial, and complete factorization counts its degree of a polynomial many roots with multiplicity of a root. It does not promise that those roots are real or that they have a simple expression.

Interlacing roots of polynomials (a1​≤b1​≤a2​≤⋯≤ad​≤bd​)

Words: 174 Articles: 2
Root of a polynomial OurBigBook.com
Two real polynomials with only real roots of a polynomial interlace when their ordered roots alternate, counting multiplicity of a root. For equal polynomial degrees, one ordering is the displayed chain; the opposite ordering is also permitted. Consecutive degrees give the analogous chain with one extra root at each end for the higher-degree polynomial. Strict interlacing uses strict inequalities. Weak interlacing permits common roots and follows as a limit of strict interlacing.
Monotonicity of polynomial critical points in their roots (∂aj​∂ξ​=∑i​(ξ−ai​)−2(ξ−aj​)−2​>0)
Words: 60
Interlacing roots of polynomials OurBigBook.com
For a monic polynomial p(x)=∏i​(x−ai​) with distinct ordered real roots of a polynomial, each critical point ξ lies between two consecutive roots by Rolle's theorem. Its logarithmic derivative gives ∑i​(ξ−ai​)−1=0. Implicit differentiation gives the displayed formula, so moving any root to the right moves every ordered critical point to the right, while the roots remain distinct. Iterating this statement for derivatives preserves componentwise ordering of their roots. Weak inequalities extend by continuity to repeated roots.
Markov interlacing lemma (p≺q⟹p(k)≺q(k))
Words: 52
Interlacing roots of polynomials OurBigBook.com
Differentiation preserves the ordering of interlacing roots of polynomials of equal or consecutive polynomial degrees. Iteration gives the result for every derivative for which both polynomials are nonconstant; common roots are allowed by a limiting argument. This is a result about the locations of roots of a polynomial, distinct from the Markov inequality for polynomial derivatives. Theorem A of Dimitar K. Dimitrov's account states the first-derivative result.

Unit-circle root (∣ξ∣=1)

Words: 33
Root of a polynomial OurBigBook.com
A root of a polynomial lying on the complex unit circle. For a numerical amplification polynomial, a simple such root gives an undamped oscillatory mode. A repeated one supplies polynomial growth in the step index and fails the root condition for a multistep method.

Positive root of a polynomial (r>0,p(r)=0)

Words: 54
Root of a polynomial OurBigBook.com
A positive root of a real polynomial p is a real number r>0 for which p(r)=0. Zero is excluded. A count of distinct positive roots counts each such number once; a count with multiplicity of a root counts a root of order m exactly m times. Multiplication by a power of x does not change either positive-root count.

Factor theorem

Words: 62
Root of a polynomial OurBigBook.com
For a polynomial f over a field, f(a)=0 exactly when X−a divides f(X). Polynomial division by the monic linear factor gives
f(X)=(X−a)q(X)+f(a).
(13)
The constant polynomial remainder is thus the value obtained by evaluation. For p(X)=X3−3X2+4, the root of a polynomial 2 gives factor X−2 and polynomial quotient X2−X−2. The latter also vanishes at 2, explaining the repeated factor. This provides a practical way to move between evaluation and factorization.

Multiplicity records how many times an object occurs when repetitions carry mathematical information.
Multiplicity of a root
Words: 152 Articles: 2
Multiplicity (mathematics) OurBigBook.com
For a nonzero polynomial over a field, the multiplicity of a root a is the largest integer m≥1 such that (X−a)m divides it. Write p(X)=(X−a)mq(X) with q(a)=0. For real polynomials, continuity keeps the sign of q fixed sufficiently near a, so an odd integer m makes the graph cross the axis and an even integer m makes it touch without crossing.
The right-hand panel above replaces (X−2)2 by (X−2)2−ε. For ε=0.04, its two roots of a polynomial are 1.8 and 2.2; for ε=−0.04, they are 2±0.2i. The unperturbed double root lies between these two cases. Small coefficient changes can therefore split a repeated root into distinct real roots or move it off the real axis, illustrating why repeated-root problems can be numerically sensitive.

A root of a polynomial is double when its multiplicity of a root is exactly two. Equivalently, p(x)=(x−x0​)2q(x) with q(x0​)=0. A generic small perturbation splits it according to square-root splitting of a double polynomial root.

Polynomial OurBigBook.com

Boolean multilinearization

Words: 41
Multilinear polynomial OurBigBook.com
Replace each positive power xid​ by xi​ in a polynomial. This gives a multilinear polynomial of no larger polynomial degree with the same values on {0,1}n. In the polynomial method in combinatorics, these functions lie in a vector space with a basis consisting of the square-free monomials of the required polynomial degrees.

Homogenisation on a uniform layer

Words: 99
Multilinear polynomial OurBigBook.com
On the uniform layer of the Boolean cube Ωr​, every multilinear polynomial of polynomial degree at most s≤r is in the span of the degree-s square-free monomials. For T⊆[n], ∣T∣=j≤s, and xT​=∏i∈T​xi​, the identity is
xT​=(s−jr−j​)−1∑S⊇T∣S∣=s​​xS​on Ωr​.
(14)
At the characteristic vector of a set A of size r, both sides vanish if T⊈A. Otherwise exactly (s−jr−j​) summands are 1. Hence the dimension of the restricted polynomial space is at most (sn​). No assertion of independence of the spanning monomials is needed, so no condition r+s≤n is required. Unlike ordinary homogenization, this operation preserves degree bounds by using the fixed-weight evaluation domain.

Multilinear reduction on the Boolean cube

Words: 60
Multilinear polynomial OurBigBook.com
Replace each positive power xia​ in a monomial by xi​ and combine equal monomials. The result is a multilinear polynomial agreeing with the original polynomial at every point of {0,1}n, because xia​=xi​ there for a≥1. Its polynomial degree does not increase. This reduction identifies polynomial functions on the Boolean lattice with their unique square-free monomial representations: uniqueness follows by successively evaluating at characteristic vectors of sets in increasing order of size.

Resultant (Res(f,g))

Words: 120 Articles: 1
Polynomial OurBigBook.com
The resultant of two univariate polynomials is the determinant of their Sylvester matrix. It vanishes exactly when the polynomials have a common root over an algebraic closure, and a nonzero resultant gives Bézout identities between the two polynomials.

Sylvester matrix

Words: 82
Resultant OurBigBook.com
For polynomials p,q of degrees m,n, the Sylvester matrix has n shifted coefficient rows of p and m shifted rows of q, with coefficients in descending-power order. It represents, after transposition, the map (A,B)↦Ap+Bq for degA<n, degB<m. Its determinant is the resultant. Its kernel is nonzero exactly when a common polynomial factor exists: divide p,q by that factor to obtain a nonzero cancelling pair; conversely, coprimality and Ap=−Bq imply p∣B, forcing the degree-bounded B and then A to vanish.

Elementary symmetric polynomial (ek​(x1​,…,xn​))

Words: 910 Articles: 6
Polynomial OurBigBook.com
The kth elementary symmetric polynomial adds every product obtained by choosing k distinct positions from x1​,…,xn​:
ek​(x1​,…,xn​)=∑1≤i1​<⋯<ik​≤n​xi1​​⋯xik​​.
(15)
The conventions are e0​=1 and ek​=0 for k>n. The positions must be distinct, but their values may coincide. Each permutation of the variables merely rearranges the summands, so this is a symmetric polynomial.
For x1​=1, x2​=2, x3​=3, we obtain e1​=1+2+3=6, e2​=1⋅2+1⋅3+2⋅3=11, and e3​=1⋅2⋅3=6. Expanding the product gives
(z−1)(z−2)(z−3)=z3−6z2+11z−6​.
(16)
In general, ∏i=1n​(z−xi​)=zn−e1​zn−1+e2​zn−2−⋯+(−1)nen​. Thus the coefficients of a monic polynomial collect elementary symmetric polynomials of its roots of a polynomial, with alternating signs. These are the Vieta formulas.[ref]

Fundamental theorem of symmetric polynomials

Words: 19
Elementary symmetric polynomial OurBigBook.com
Every symmetric polynomial over a commutative ring has a unique expression as a polynomial in the elementary symmetric polynomials.

Newton's identities (mem​=∑r=1m​(−1)r−1em−r​pr​)

Words: 736 Articles: 4
Elementary symmetric polynomial OurBigBook.com
Newton's identities let two different summaries of the same polynomial roots talk to each other. Elementary symmetric polynomials record products of distinct root positions; power sums record sums of individual powers, pr​=∑i=1n​xir​. Either can be easier to obtain in a particular problem. The identities turn one into the other, often avoiding any need to find the individual polynomial roots.
Write e0​=1 and em​=0 for m>n. For every positive integer m, the identity is
mem​=r=1∑m​(−1)r−1em−r​pr​​.
(17)
It is a polynomial identity over the integers, so it remains true on substitution in any commutative ring. To solve it for em​ by division, however, m must have a multiplicative inverse. Over a field of characteristic zero, the first n power sums recover every elementary symmetric polynomial. The same recovery works when the positive characteristic of a field is greater than n; small characteristic needs care.[ref]
The first three relations are e1​=p1​, 2e2​=e1​p1​−p2​, and 3e3​=e2​p1​−e1​p2​+p3​. When division by two and three is permitted, this becomes
e1​=p1​,e2​=2p12​−p2​​,e3​=6p13​−3p1​p2​+2p3​​.
(18)
For the three roots 1,2,3, their power sums are p1​=6, p2​=14, and p3​=36. The formulas give e2​=(36−14)/2=11 and e3​=(216−252+72)/6=6, recovering the polynomial z3−6z2+11z−6 from aggregate data.
The beauty is that the summaries do not depend on the order of the polynomial roots. In symmetric polynomials, one can work with quantities that survive every relabeling; in linear algebra, traces of matrix powers give the same kind of aggregate information about eigenvalues. The identities convert those summaries into coefficients of a characteristic polynomial.
A short derivation packages the identities into a formal power series. Let E(t)=∏i​(1+xi​t)=∑m≥0​em​tm. Since its constant coefficient is one, it has an inverse as a formal power series, and its formal derivative satisfies
E(t)E′(t)​=∑i​1+xi​txi​​=∑r≥1​(−1)r−1pr​tr−1.
(19)
Multiply by E(t) and compare the coefficient of tm−1. This gives Newton's identities without a convergence assumption or division by m. The division issue arises only when using them to recover em​. The logarithmic-derivative approach is also developed in Newton's Identities (January 2019 notes) by Milan Mossé (§4, pp. 6–8).
The alternate name Newton-Girard identities recalls Albert Girard's earlier work. A modern historical account credits formulas through sixth powers to Albert Girard in 1629 and discusses their later appearance in Isaac Newton's Arithmetica universalis.[ref] This citation refers to that account; the original historical editions have not been inspected here.

For the monic polynomial q(z)=zn−e1​zn−1+⋯+(−1)nen​, its root power sums satisfy
pm​=e1​pm−1​−e2​pm−2​+⋯+(−1)n+1en​pm−n​,m>n.
(20)
Each root obeys q(xi​)=0. Multiplying that equation by xim−n​ and summing over root positions proves the recurrence relation. The first n power sums are initialized by Newton's identities; their later values require only this fixed-order recurrence. For q(z)=z3−6z2+11z−6, it gives p4​=6⋅36−11⋅14+6⋅6=98. Directly, 14+24+34=98. No new root-solving step is needed.[ref]

Characteristic polynomial from traces of powers (pk​=tr(Ak))

Words: 83
Newton's identities OurBigBook.com
For a complex n×n matrix A, tr(Ak) is the sum of the kth powers of its eigenvalues, counted with algebraic multiplicity. This does not require diagonalizability: a similar upper triangular matrix has the eigenvalues on its diagonal, and taking powers raises those diagonal entries to their corresponding powers. Newton's identities therefore recover its characteristic polynomial from the first n such traces.
For the Jordan block A=(20​12​), trA=4 and tr(A2)=8. Hence e1​=4 and e2​=(42−8)/2=4, giving det(zI−A)=z2−4z+4=(z−2)2. The repeated eigenvalue is recovered even though this matrix is not diagonalizable.[ref]

Root sensitivity in power-sum reconstruction (p1​=2, p2​=2+δ⟹x1,2​=1±δ/2​)

Words: 112
Newton's identities OurBigBook.com
Exact reconstruction does not promise that small errors in power sums produce proportionally small errors in individual polynomial roots. For two roots, let p1​=2 and p2​=2+δ. Newton's identities give e1​=2 and e2​=1−δ/2, so the monic polynomial is (z−1)2−δ/2. Its polynomial roots are 1±δ/2​. A zero value of δ gives a multiple root; positive δ splits it into two real roots, and negative δ splits it into a complex-conjugate pair.
With δ=2ε2>0, the second power sum changes by 2ε2 while each polynomial root moves by ε. The ratio 1/(2ε) grows without bound as ε tends to zero. Thus coefficients can stay close while individual root locations are more sensitive. This is a reason to distinguish recovering coefficients by Newton's identities from subsequently approximating the polynomial roots.

Newton identities in positive characteristic

Words: 74
Newton's identities OurBigBook.com
The polynomial identities remain true in positive characteristic of a field, but recovering elementary symmetric polynomials by division can fail. In the prime field F2​ of characteristic two, the root lists (0,0) and (1,1) have the same power sum zero for every positive exponent: 0k+0k=0 and 1k+1k=0. Their monic polynomials differ, however: z2 and (z−1)2=z2+1. Thus even all positive power sums need not determine the polynomial when its degree meets the characteristic. The relation 2e2​=e1​p1​−p2​ becomes 0=0 and supplies no value for e2​.

An irreducible polynomial is a nonconstant polynomial that cannot be written as a product of two nonconstant polynomials over its coefficient field. Over a general integral domain, neither factor may be a unit.

Irreducible polynomial OurBigBook.com
If f is an irreducible polynomial over a field F, then a nonzero residue [g] modulo (f) has gcd(f,g)=1. The Euclidean algorithm supplies uf+vg=1, giving inverse [v] for [g]. Thus the quotient ring F[X]/(f) is a field. If degf=d and F has q elements, polynomial division supplies exactly qd residue classes.

The polynomial remainder is the polynomial r in polynomial division q=Qs+r. Division by X−a has a constant polynomial remainder q(a), as expressed by the factor theorem.

Polynomial long division

Polynomial division OurBigBook.com
To divide q by a nonzero polynomial Q over a field, subtract the multiple of Q that cancels the leading term of the current remainder, and add that multiple to the quotient. Each step strictly decreases the remainder degree, so the process terminates with q=Qs+r and degr<degQ. If two such pairs existed, Q(s−s′)=r′−r would have degree both at least degQ and less than degQ, unless both differences vanished.

Degree of a polynomial (deg)

Words: 145 Articles: 2
Polynomial OurBigBook.com
The degree of a nonzero polynomial is the largest exponent of a monomial with a nonzero coefficient. Thus X3−3X2+4 has degree three, while any nonzero constant polynomial has degree zero. The zero polynomial is treated separately in degree statements.
Over an integral domain, polynomial degrees add under multiplication: deg(pq)=degp+degq for nonzero factors, because the product of their leading coefficients cannot vanish. Under addition, cancellation may lower the degree: (X2+1)+(−X2+X)=X+1. This explains why degree is reliable for counting factors and bounding polynomial roots, but cannot always be inferred from the degrees of summands alone.
